questions.worked_solution:
First, we express $y$ as the composite function

$$
y={log}_{5}⁡(u),\,u=5x.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}=\frac{1}{u\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)},\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=5.
$$

We now apply the chain rule, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}u}\cdot \frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x} \\  & =\frac{1}{u\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot 5 \\  & =\frac{1}{(5x)\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}\cdot 5 \\  & =\frac{\cancel{5}}{\cancel{5}x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)} \\  & =\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}⁡(5)}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Given that the line $y=-4x+k$ does **not** intersect the parabola $y={x}^{2}+5,$ what is the range of possible values of $k?$
questions.worked_solution:
To determine whether the line $y=-4x+k$ intersects the parabola $y={x}^{2}+5,$ we need to solve the following system of equations for the two curves:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}y={x}^{2}+5 \\ y=-4x+k\end{aligned}
$$

Setting the equations equal to one another and writing in standard form, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+5 & =-4x+k \\ {x}^{2}+4x+5-k & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we solve this equation using the quadratic formula with $a=1,\,b=4,$ and $c=5-k:$

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{{4}^{2}-4(1)(5-k)}}{2(1)} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{16-20+4k}}{2} \\  & =\frac{-4\pm \sqrt{4k-4}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the line and parabola do not intersect, our quadratic equation must have no real solutions; hence, the expression inside the square root must be negative.
Setting up and solving this inequality, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}4k-4 & <0 \\ 4k & <4 \\ k & <1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the range of possible values of $k$ is $k<1.$

questions.problem:
Consider two sets of $28$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{28},$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{28}.$ You are given that

$$
\begin{aligned} & {\sum }_{i=1}^{28}{x}_{i}=560,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{28}{y}_{i}=588, \\  & {\sum }_{i=1}^{28}{x}_{i}^{2}=10\,920,\,{\sum }_{i=1}^{28}{y}_{i}^{2}=13\,220.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate the sum of the squared deviations from the mean for the points ${y}_{i}.$

${S}_{yy}=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
Given a set of $n$ paired observations ${x}_{1},{x}_{2},…,{x}_{n}$ and ${y}_{1},{y}_{2},…,{y}_{n},$ the sum of squared deviations from the mean for the data ${y}_{i}$ can be calculated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{yy} & ={\sum }_{i=1}^{n}({y}_{i}-\overset{―}{y})^{2} \\  & ={\sum }_{i}{y}_{i}^{2}-\frac{1}{n}{({\sum }_{i=1}^{n}{y}_{i})}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the given statistics in the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{S}_{yy} & =13\,220-\frac{1}{28}(588)^{2} \\  & =13\,220-12\,348 \\  & =872.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{1}{{m}^{2}-9}÷\frac{2}{m+3},

$$

$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14274204/assets/bd3aa904b0d5a686fe8107e05d5723ea563539dc2983fdae6cc424e40a0cf87b.png)

A teacher collects information on the age ($x,$ in years)  and shoe size ($y$)  from a group of children in an elementary school. The scatter plot for the data and the corresponding linear regression line are shown above.

According to the regression model, what is the residual for the highlighted datapoint?
questions.worked_solution:
The residual equals the difference between the actual value of the dependent variable and the value estimated using the linear regression model:

$$
\text{Residual}=\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated}
$$

 

The highlighted datapoint has coordinates $(9,2).$ So, our actual value is $y=2.$

On the other hand, the point on the regression line that corresponds to $x=9$ has the $y$-coordinate $3.$ So, our estimated value is $\overset{^}{y}=3.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/linear/14274204/assets/24812897045394f5ebeb1285bbcb7a6745afdca8372633431f6c0b16f5b0ecbc.png)

As a result, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Residual} & =\text{Actual}-\text{Estimated} \\  & =y-\overset{^}{y} \\  & =2-3 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the residual is $-1.$

questions.problem: The pressure $P$ of a gas kept at a fixed temperature varies inversely with the volume $V$ it occupies. When $V=2\,{\text{m}}^{3}$, the pressure is $P=1$ megapascal ($\text{MPa}$). Find the pressure when $V=0.5\,{\text{m}}^{3}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The pressure $P$ is inversely proportional to the volume $V,$ so we have

$$
P=\frac{k}{V},
$$

where $k$ is the constant of variation.

We are told that when the volume is $V=2\,{\text{m}}^{3},$ the pressure is $P=1$ megapascal ($\text{MPa}$). We can use this information to solve for $k$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =\frac{k}{2} \\ 2\cdot 1 & =k \\ 2 & =k\end{aligned}
$$

We now have the equation

$$
P=\frac{2}{V}.
$$

We can use this equation to find the pressure when the volume is $V=0.5\,{\text{m}}^{3},$ as follows:

$$
P=\frac{2}{0.5}=4
$$

Therefore, the pressure of the gas when $V=0.5\,{\text{m}}^{3}$ is $4\,\text{MPa}.$

questions.problem: The point $P(-6,4)$ is acted on by a reflection across the $y$-axis followed by the translation  $(x,y)↦(x-7,y-3).$ What is the image of $P$ under this transformation?
questions.worked_solution:
Let's recall the functional representations of our two transformations:

- A reflection across the $y$-axis can be represented by the function 

$$
(x,y)↦(-x,y).
$$

- Our translation is represented by the function 

$$
(x,y)↦(x-7,y-3).
$$

Let's apply the given transformations to the point $P$ using our functions:

First, we apply the reflection. The image of the point $(-6,4)$ under the reflection is

$$
(-6,4)↦(6,4).
$$

 

Then, we apply the translation. The image of the point $(6,4)$ under the translation is

$$
(6,4)↦(6-7,4-3)=(-1,1).
$$

Therefore, the resulting point is $(-1,1).$

$$

Notice that all of the terms in our expression have a common factor of $8.$ To simplify the computation, we can factor out the $8,$ as follows:

$$
8{z}^{4}-128=8\cdot {z}^{4}-8\cdot 16=8({z}^{4}-16)
$$

The expression in parentheses can be written as a difference of squares:

$$
8({z}^{4}-16)=8({({z}^{2})}^{2}-{4}^{2})

Now, we factor our expression using the difference of squares formula:

$$
8({({z}^{2})}^{2}-{4}^{2})=8({z}^{2}+4)({z}^{2}-4)
$$

Finally, we notice that the expression in the second set of parentheses is also a difference of squares. Therefore, the expression can be factored further, as follows:

$$
